question: Who regulates insurers: states, Treasury, the Fed or global bodies?
answer: Mostly the states. Treasury's own 2026 Federal Insurance Office report says the primary regulators of the business of insurance are the 50 states, the District of Columbia and five U.S. territories. Treasury's Federal Insurance Office monitors, advises, represents and administers bounded federal roles; the Financial Stability Oversight Council monitors system risk and can designate a nonbank under section 113; Federal Reserve insurance-group supervision applies only to covered holding companies and designated nonbanks. Global bodies write shared standards, but IAIS adoption is not self-executing state or federal law and does not itself intervene in a group.

sections.title: Each rule-maker and supervisor, in the hub's words
sections.sub: The 13 boxes of the hub's top-down lens, column by column: what each one does, what it controls and what not to infer.

items.title: Congress, state legislatures and courts
items.sub: Sovereign law · Create the legal perimeter, public programs and failure rules
kv: Define insurance charters, solvency authority, taxes, benefit systems, receivership, assessments and public risk-sharing programs.
Statute and binding judicial interpretation sit above models, guidance, contracts and company practice.
A proposal, speech, model law or international standard is not operative domestic law.

items.title: State insurance commissioners
items.sub: State system · Primary legal-entity supervisors of the business of insurance
kv: License, examine and enforce against domestic insurers; control reserves, capital, material transactions, dividends and receivership under state law.
The domiciliary commissioner controls the licensed legal entity; other states retain market and consumer authority within their laws.
State primacy does not eliminate federal securities, benefit, financial-stability, tax or public-program authority.

items.title: NAIC coordination and accreditation
items.sub: State system · Builds model law, accounting, RBC, data and peer standards
kv: Coordinates state regulators and maintains solvency tools, statutory accounting, model laws, filing instructions and accreditation expectations.
Member regulators adopt NAIC work through their own lawful processes and use shared systems in supervision.
The NAIC is not a federal insurance ministry; model adoption does not create identical law in every state.

items.title: Lead state, GCC, ORSA and liquidity stress test
items.sub: State system · Adds group and macroprudential windows around legal-entity walls
kv: Coordinates holding-company supervision and examines enterprise risk, group capital location, liquidity and affiliate exposure.
Lead state defines the group scope with other domiciliary regulators; confidential filings and supervisory action remain distinct.
Group capital is not automatically fungible and an ORSA is not the legal-entity RBC intervention trigger.

items.title: Treasury Federal Insurance Office
items.sub: Federal perimeter · Monitors, advises, represents and administers bounded federal roles
kv: Monitors systemic gaps and access, advises Treasury, represents the United States internationally, supports TRIP and can recommend FSOC designation.
Its powers arise under Title V and covered-agreement statutes; important health-insurance limits remain.
FIO generally does not charter insurers, approve rates or supervise every insurance legal entity.
Research notes in the package (internal files, not linked)
Big insurance monetary and government control map; Insurance source watchboard; Cross-border supervision, market structure and resolution map

items.title: Financial Stability Oversight Council
items.sub: Federal perimeter · Monitors system risk and can designate a nonbank under section 113
kv: Identifies financial-stability threats and can bring a qualifying nonbank financial company under Federal Reserve supervision and prudential standards.
Designation requires the statutory determination and the Council's process; monitoring and annual-report discussion are earlier states.
A vulnerability, working-group review or FIO recommendation is not a designation, distress finding or bailout.

Big insurance monetary and government control map

items.title: Federal Reserve insurance-group supervision
items.sub: Federal perimeter · Applies only to covered holding companies and designated nonbanks
kv: Supervises covered depository-institution holding companies significantly engaged in insurance and applies the Building Block Approach where required.
Regulation Q aggregates capital frameworks while preserving underlying state insurance and federal bank building blocks.
The Federal Reserve does not supervise every insurer or replace state legal-entity solvency authority.
Research notes in the package (internal files, not linked)
Big insurance monetary and government control map

items.title: SEC, DOL, CMS, PBGC, FHFA, NRC, FAA and other federal perimeters
items.sub: Federal perimeter · Regulate named products, benefits, liquidity systems and public guarantees
kv: Reach variable products and securities, ERISA plans, federal health programs, pension guarantees, FHLBank membership, taxes, sanctions, transport, environmental and strategic-liability regimes.
Each agency owns its statute, covered entity, instrument and enforcement or payment record.
Functional federal authority is not one consolidated insurance regulator.

items.title: IAIS, ComFrame and Insurance Capital Standard
items.sub: Global & group · Create a common group-supervision language for IAIGs
kv: Set international supervisory principles, group standards and the ICS prescribed capital requirement for internationally active insurance groups.
Domestic supervisors implement and IAIS assessment tests comparable prudence and intervention.
IAIS adoption is not self-executing state or federal law and does not itself intervene in a group.

items.title: IAIS Holistic Framework and FSB monitoring
items.sub: Global & group · Tracks sector and activity channels beyond a static entity list
kv: Focuses on liquidity, counterparty exposure, recovery, resolution and macroprudential risk across firms and activities.
IAIS global monitoring and jurisdictional supervisory responses create separate records.
Framework monitoring is not a G-SII designation, domestic rule or finding of distress.
Research notes in the package (internal files, not linked)
Big insurance monetary and government control map; Cross-border supervision, market structure and resolution map

items.title: Foreign group and reinsurance supervisors
items.sub: Global & group · Control legal entities and groups in Bermuda, Cayman, UK, EU and other regimes
kv: License and supervise foreign insurers and reinsurers and participate in colleges and information exchange.
Home-jurisdiction law and group-supervisor decisions govern their entities and capital standards.
An MOU, reciprocal-jurisdiction status or cooperation statement is not shared fiscal backing or treaty approval.

items.title: Insurance holding company and wider group
items.sub: Global & group · Owns subsidiaries and coordinates strategy above protected legal entities
kv: May contain insurers, reinsurers, banks, asset managers, service companies and special-purpose vehicles.
Ownership and governance create influence, while regulated-entity walls constrain dividends, transactions and capital movement.
A group brand is not the policy issuer, asset owner, reinsurer or freely accessible pool of cash.

items.title: Licensed insurers, reinsurers and captives
items.sub: Private balance sheets · Separate balance sheets hold separate promises and capital
kv: Write policies, assume treaties, hold reserves and own assets under their domiciliary regimes.
Each entity's charter, licence, contracts, statutory accounts and supervisor define its legal perimeter.
Consolidated presentation does not erase entity-level obligations, collateral or creditor priority.

sections.title: The ten levels of the U.S. insurance constitution
sections.sub: The study's own table: who holds which power, the record that proves it, and its limit. FIO's September 2026 report states the constitutional split plainly: the primary regulators of the business of insurance are the 50 states, the District of Columbia and five U.S. territories, while federal law creates important financial-stability, securities, benefit-plan, tax, public-program and international roles.

catalog_context.title: How insurers invest trillions, move risk and share losses with government
catalog_context.answer: U.S. insurance runs through many separate regulators, very large insurer balance sheets, reinsurance and public loss programs that together work as one system. Each authority, company, contract and payment still keeps its own legal identity and timing.
